subject: Art & Design
title: Iteration: Good Design Is Redesign
description: A 60-second lesson on Iteration: Good Design Is Redesign.

hook.text: The first version of the Google logo was made in GIMP in 1998. It took 17 years of iteration to reach today's.

buildup.text: No first draft is the final design. Iteration means refining through rounds of feedback and testing.

discovery.text: Show rough work early. Getting feedback on a polished piece wastes the time spent polishing.

twist.text: The hardest part of iteration isn't making changes — it's letting go of ideas you're attached to.

climax.text: Set iteration limits. Three rounds of revision is standard. Without limits, perfection becomes the enemy.

punchline.text: Design isn't done when it's perfect. It's done when it works.

quiz.question: Why should you show rough work early?
options: Feedback on polished work wastes the time spent polishing

details.summary: Iteration — designing, testing, learning, and redesigning repeatedly — is how good design actually happens. No design is right on the first attempt. Professional designers expect multiple rounds of refinement, using each version to discover problems and opportunities invisible in the previous one.
details.whyItMatters: The myth of the inspired genius creating perfection in one stroke damages real design practice. Understanding iteration normalizes revision and recognizes that the design process — not a single flash of insight — produces quality work.
takeaways: Good design emerges through multiple rounds of refinement
Each iteration reveals problems invisible in previous versions
The process, not a single insight, produces quality work

faq.question: How many iterations does a typical design project need?
faq.answer: Three to five major iterations is common for professional projects. Initial concepts explore direction, middle rounds refine the chosen approach, and final rounds polish details.

faq.question: When should you stop iterating?
faq.answer: When additional changes produce diminishing returns and the design meets its documented objectives. Perfectionism can become counter-productive. The best designers know when a design is 'done enough' — serving its purpose effectively even if it could theoretically be improved further.
